t.2.89.1: Then, having come down from the mountain, the lord of Kosala showed Maithilī the lovely river Mandākinī with its clear, auspicious waters.
t.2.89.2: And lotus-eyed Rāma spoke to the daughter of the king of Videha, the fair-hipped lady whose face was like the lovely moon.
t.2.89.3: Behold the river Mandākinī, lovely, with its many-hued sandbanks, frequented by geese and cranes, and richly adorned with flowers.
t.2.89.5: These lovely bathing places, whose waters have now been drunk by herds of deer and are muddied, awaken delight in me.
t.2.89.4: Behold her, surrounded by flowering and fruit-bearing trees of many kinds growing along her banks, shining on every side like the lotus pond of the king of kings.
t.2.89.6: And see, beloved, the sages, wearing matted locks and deerskins, with bark garments as their upper cloth, plunge at the proper time into the river Mandākinī.
t.2.89.7: These other sages, O large-eyed one, firm in their vows, worship the Sun as a religious observance, with their arms raised upward.
t.2.89.8: With its trees, their tops tossed by the wind, scattering leaves and blossoms all around the river, the mountain seems almost to be dancing.
t.2.89.10: Look at the heaps of flowers shaken loose by the wind and scattered far and wide; and look at the others, floating and bobbing in the midst of the water.
t.2.89.9: Behold the river Mandākinī, here with waters clear as gems, there graced with sandy banks, and elsewhere thronged with Siddhas.
t.2.89.11: And onto those places, which ring with exceedingly sweet sounds, O fair one, the birds named after the chariot-wheel alight, warbling auspicious songs.
t.2.89.12: O lovely one, I consider the sight of Citrakūṭa and of the Mandākinī to be greater than dwelling in the city, and all the more so because I behold you.
t.2.89.14: And, Sītā, plunge into this Mandākinī as you would with a friend, O lovely lady, sinking the red lotuses and the blue lotuses beneath the water.
t.2.89.13: Plunge with me into this river, whose waters are ever stirred by Siddhas who have shaken off all impurity and are endowed with austerity, self-restraint and tranquility.
t.2.89.15: O lady, always regard the wild beasts as the townsfolk, this mountain as Ayodhyā, and this river as the Sarayū.
t.2.89.16: Righteous Lakṣmaṇa, who stands firm in my command, and you too, Vaidehī, ever agreeable to me, together bring me joy.
t.2.89.17: Bathing at the three times of the day and living on honey, roots and fruits, I now long neither for Ayodhyā nor for the kingdom, being here with you.
t.2.89.18: For there is no one who, having come to this lovely river, stirred by herds of elephants, its waters drunk by elephants, lions and monkeys, and adorned with flower-bearing trees in full bloom, would not become happy.
t.2.89.19: Thus speaking many fitting words about the river, Rāma, the one who made the line of Raghu prosper, roamed with his beloved as his companion over delightful Citrakūṭa, which gleamed dark like the collyrium of the eyes.
